# IAM Identity Center, Directory Service and Cognito: say it

<!-- speak:start id=identity-federation-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** What is the difference between IAM Identity Center and Cognito? Both look like sign-in to me.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both sign people in. IAM Identity Center is for your employees and your AWS accounts. Cognito is for the people who use your app.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both sign people in, but to different places: your AWS accounts, or your app.

The difference is who signs in.

It works like this. IAM Identity Center is for your own engineers.

They sign in once and get a role in each assigned AWS account.

It doesn't create IAM users. It creates a role from each permission set.

Cognito is for the people who use your app.

A user pool signs them in and gives your app tokens.

The thing to watch is that Cognito can't be the identity source of IAM Identity Center. Keep the paths separate.

In your case, your engineers go through IAM Identity Center.

The bank's supervisors sign in to a user pool through their bank's provider.

The bank checks their passwords, so Callvale doesn't store them.

Does anyone outside Callvale need an AWS account, or only the dashboard?

**Skeleton.** both sign in, different places / engineers: role in each account / app users: user pool tokens / Cognito is no identity source

**Must say.**

- IAM Identity Center gives employees single sign-on to the AWS accounts that are assigned to them.
- IAM Identity Center does not create IAM users; it creates an IAM role for each permission set in each assigned account.
- Cognito gives customer identity and access management (CIAM) to the web and mobile apps that you build.
- A user pool signs users in and issues JSON web tokens to your app; an identity pool exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials.
- Cognito is not a supported identity source for IAM Identity Center.

**Do not say.**

- "Cognito can be the identity source of IAM Identity Center". Say: Cognito is not a supported identity source for IAM Identity Center. Employees reach AWS accounts through IAM Identity Center.
- "IAM Identity Center creates an IAM user for each engineer in each account". Say: IAM Identity Center does not create IAM users and groups. It creates an IAM role for each permission set in each assigned account.
- "the app can call Amazon S3 with the user pool token". Say: A user pool issues tokens for your app or API. An identity pool exchanges the token for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If an engineer leaves, how fast does the AWS access end? Disable the user and remove the assignments. A role session that is already open can last up to 12 hours. To end it sooner in member accounts, add the user to a Deny in a service control policy and keep it for 12 hours. A service control policy does not reach the management account.
- When a second bank brings a different identity provider, does the app need new code? No. The user pool is a service provider to each outside provider and an identity provider to your app. Your app keeps working with one set of JWTs.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=identity-federation-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Our users are in Active Directory in our office. Do we need AD Connector or AWS Managed Microsoft AD?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** For sign-in to AWS applications, use AD Connector. For RDS for SQL Server, use AWS Managed Microsoft AD: AD Connector does not serve it.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: AD Connector for sign-in, and Managed AD for Windows workloads.

It works like this. AD Connector is a proxy.

It forwards each sign-in to the domain controllers in your office.

Your directory data stays on those domain controllers.

AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real Active Directory that AWS runs for you.

You connect it to your office with a trust.

The thing to watch is your Windows workloads. RDS for SQL Server doesn't work with AD Connector, and neither does FSx for Windows.

AD Connector also needs a VPN or Direct Connect to your office.

In your case, if people only sign in to AWS applications, start with AD Connector.

For RDS for SQL Server, choose Managed AD. FSx for Windows can also join your own domain.

Which systems in AWS need your directory?

**Skeleton.** proxy or real directory / AD Connector keeps no copy / RDS and FSx: not AD Connector / VPN or Direct Connect

**Must say.**

- AD Connector is a proxy that forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises domain controllers.
- With AD Connector, the directory data stays on your domain controllers; AWS does not replicate any of it.
- AWS Managed Microsoft AD is an actual Microsoft Windows Server Active Directory that AWS manages, and it can trust the on-premises directory.
- AD Connector is not compatible with Amazon RDS for SQL Server, and Amazon FSx for Windows File Server does not support it; FSx joins Managed AD or your own AD.
- AD Connector needs a VPN connection or AWS Direct Connect to the on-premises network.

**Do not say.**

- "AD Connector copies your users and passwords to AWS". Say: AD Connector forwards sign-in requests to your domain controllers. AWS does not replicate any of your directory data.
- "Simple AD can trust your office directory". Say: Simple AD does not support trust relationships. Use AWS Managed Microsoft AD for a trust.
- "RDS for SQL Server can use AD Connector". Say: AD Connector is not compatible with RDS SQL Server. Of the Directory Service options, use AWS Managed Microsoft AD.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If we add a one-way trust for RDS, will IAM Identity Center sign-in work too? No. IAM Identity Center requires a two-way trust, and one-way trusts do not work with it. Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS and Amazon FSx work with either a one-way or a two-way trust.
- We have a parent domain and child domains. Is one AD Connector enough? No. AD Connector does not support transitive trusts. Each on-premises domain, including each child domain, needs its own AD Connector.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
